content.key_idea: Blocks in charge of the same shard form a pointer chain across rounds, so once a leader commits a block far enough along that chain, its causal history is forced to include a proper prefix of the whole chain, giving every block in it a determinate order before commitment.
content.reading_order: left to right by round (1 through 6), scanning down the four node rows within each round; colour identifies each block's shard (green k1, blue k2) or leader role (red), and pointer arrows trace each block back to the previous round's block in charge of the same shard

summary: This figure is a worked-example grid of protocol rounds (columns 1-6) by nodes (rows Node 1-4) in Lemonshark's asynchronous DAG-BFT. Coloured blocks mark which node is in charge of which shard's block each round: green blocks (b1^1, b1^2, b1^3, b1^4) belong to shard k1, blue blocks (b2^1, b2^2, b2^3, b2^4) belong to shard k2, and two red blocks (b', b'') are leader blocks that later commit portions of the DAG. Pointer arrows connect each shard's block to the block that was in charge of the same shard in an earlier round, forming a recursive chain per shard. The figure illustrates Lemonshark's core argument for early finality: a committing leader far along such a chain is forced to include a proper prefix of the whole chain in its causal history, giving every block in it a determinate execution order before commitment.
